messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Vignette:
At 42, Meera Patel came to treatment exhausted by the effort of getting through ordinary days. She is a married South Asian American woman who works as a maid, cleaning private homes and a small office building on weekends. When she first tried to describe what had happened to her, her account came in broken pieces. She would begin, stop, shake her head, and say that the whole thing disappeared just when she got close to it, as if her mind pushed it away before it could become complete. She knew the facts in outline: for months, a man began following her during her commute and near the apartment complex where she worked. But when she tried to tell it straight through, she could not hold it in order. Certain moments came back sharply and bodily, while the rest felt blocked off.

What she could describe most clearly was the atmosphere of those encounters. The man would appear after she left work, often in the late afternoon, after she had finished cleaning apartments. He would stand too close, stare at her body in a way that made her feel stripped and cornered, and speak to her as if she owed him attention. On more than one occasion she smelled alcohol on him before she fully registered his face. She remembered the stale, sour smell of liquor mixing with the chemical lemon scent of cleaning products still on her hands. One day, after hurrying away from him with her jaw clenched and her mouth dry, she became aware of the metallic, bitter taste in her mouth so strongly that even now, when the memory breaks through, she can taste it again. Over time the stalking became less ambiguous to her. He showed up outside places where he should not have known to find her, watched her in silence, and made comments that turned her body into something for him to inspect. What frightened her most was not only that he was there, but the certainty that he had been paying attention to her routines.

In the weeks and months that followed, Meera did not feel safe even when the man was not present. At home with her husband, she began checking the front door, then the windows, then returning again a few minutes later to make sure she had really locked them. She said silence in the apartment had become unbearable. If the hallway outside went quiet or the street noise dropped away, she felt a jolt in her chest, as if danger had moved closer. Even inside her own home she stayed on guard, listening for steps, a knock, a voice outside the door. She had come to believe that being relaxed was risky, that something bad could happen in the exact moment she let herself settle.

Her work kept putting her into situations that touched the worst parts of the experience. In clients’ homes she often cleaned bedrooms and bathrooms alone, and if a male resident looked at her in a way that felt lingering or appraising, her whole body tightened. She would keep her eyes down, finish as fast as possible, and later replay the interaction repeatedly. Before speaking to clients, building staff, or even neighbors, she rehearsed what she would say: how to sound brief, polite, not inviting, not rude, not noticeable. She wanted every interaction controlled in advance. Physical pain could also set her off. If her shoulder or lower back ached after scrubbing tubs or carrying supplies, the sensation could pull her toward the memory before she fully understood why, and then she would fight to shut it down before it unfolded.

Outside work, her life narrowed. She stopped seeing friends because being out felt exposed and because she could not bear casual questions about how she was doing. She spent much of her energy worrying about the safety of people she loved. If her husband was late answering his phone, her mind rushed immediately to images of something terrible having happened. If a relative was traveling, she felt unable to rest until she heard they were home. To her, this vigilance seemed like responsibility, the only way to be prepared.

By the time she sought help, Meera was worn down by living as if danger were always about to announce itself from behind a quiet hallway or an unopened door. What finally brought her in was a recent moment at work when a client’s guest, smelling of alcohol, thanked her while looking her up and down; afterward she locked herself in the bathroom, shaking, with that old bitter taste suddenly in her mouth. She told the therapist she was tired of arranging her life around fear and tired of not being able to tell her own story from beginning to end. At the same time, she was afraid that if she let herself remember it fully, it would become overwhelming and she would never feel safe again.
